title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarking Suite & Runbooks
author: Alicia Martinez
content:
Overview

This document consolidates our serving runtime reference material: architecture overview, kernel scheduling policies, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes highlights, known issues, and day-to-day runbooks for on-call engineers. It is intended for engineers owning the serving runtime, SREs, performance engineers, and release leads.

Purpose and scope
- Provide a single authoritative reference for runtime architecture and scheduling decisions.
- Describe standard profiling and benchmarking procedures for regression detection and capacity planning.
- Document operational runbooks for common incidents and maintenance tasks.
- Track relevant release notes and outstanding known issues.

Audience and ownership
- Primary: eng-serving-runtime team (owners of runtime code, kernel selection, and perf tests)
- Secondary: eng-sre (capacity and runbooks), eng-infra (deployment tooling), product (release sign-off)
- Owner: serving-runtime core team (oncall alias: runtime-oncall@redwood.example.com)

1) Runtime architecture (concise reference)

Summary
The serving runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine that exposes a unified HTTP/gRPC endpoint for text generation, chat, and embeddings. The runtime consists of the following logical layers:
- Frontend (request ingestion, policy routing)
- Dispatcher (worker selection, KV/prefix cache lookup)
- Execution layer (kernel runtime, GPU memory manager, quantized operators)
- Persistence & Telemetry (metrics, traces, audit logs)

Key components and ownership
- request-proxy (ingest + auth) — team: eng-platform
- runtime-dispatcher (scheduling, batching, cache) — team: eng-serving-runtime (owner)
- model-executor (kernel selection + execution) — team: eng-serving-runtime
- kv-cache (in-memory prefix+KV cache, optional Redis backing) — team: eng-serving-runtime
- telemetry-agent (metrics, traces, pprof exporters) — team: eng-platform

SLOs and capacity targets
- 95th-percentile token-generation latency (text-gen requests, short context <= 128 tokens): <= 70ms
- 99th-percentile tail latency (99p): <= 250ms for hosted tier
- Throughput per GPU (A100-80GB equivalent): baseline 12k tokens/sec for gpt-3 style models (non-quantized); expect 1.8x improvement for 4-bit quantized variants
- Availability SLO: 99.95% for dedicated pools, 99.9% for hosted API

Model variant and fallback policy
- Models are registered with capability and compatibility tags (e.g., causal-lm/v1, seq2seq/v1, kv-cache/compatible).
- Smart routing prioritizes: 1) pinned model on customer pool, 2) compatible local variant (quantized/FP16), 3) regional fallback, 4) hosted burst pool.

2) Kernel selection and scheduling (design and operational controls)

Goals
- Maximize single-GPU throughput while meeting tail latency SLOs.
- Avoid fragmentation of GPU memory and reduce kernel launch overhead.
- Provide predictable latency by controlling batch size and preemption windows.

Scheduling primitives
- Scheduling unit: request-shard (group of requests with compatible model, seq_len bucket, and priority).
- Batch windows: adjustable in ms; default is 8ms for low-latency tiers, 40ms for throughput-optimized tiers.
- Preemption policy: soft preemption for low-priority batches (eviction of queued batches older than 2x batch window); hard preemption only during node reclamation (must be accompanied by fallback).

Kernel selection heuristics (runtime-dispatcher -> model-executor)
1. Sequence-length bucketing: select kernel path optimized for the seq_len bucket (<=64, 65-256, 257-2048).
2. Precision preference: prefer quantized kernel if model variant supports it and quality budget permits; fallback to FP16 if latency constraints not met.
3. Memory layout: choose kernels that minimize activation duplication (favor single-stream fused kernels for long contexts).
4. Hardware capability check: select kernels exposed for sm80, sm90, or newer; runtime contains capability matrix to avoid forbidden kernels.

Operational knobs (configurable per pool/model)
- batch_window_ms (string value, ms)
- max_batch_tokens (string value)
- allow_quantized (string: true/false)
- preemption_threshold_ms (string, ms)
- kv_cache_enabled (string: true/false)

Example config snippet (YAML-like text)

pool_config:
  name: example-dedicated-pool
  batch_window_ms: "8"
  max_batch_tokens: "4096"
  allow_quantized: "true"
  preemption_threshold_ms: "16"
  kv_cache_enabled: "true"

3) Profiling playbook (how to collect and interpret signals)

When to profile
- New kernel landed in model-executor or fused-op added
- Regression alert fires from CI/benchmarks or console (>=5% latency increase or >=10% throughput drop)
- Customer-reported high tail latency with reproducible workload

Quick checklist
1. Reproduce workload in staging (use same model and batch config). Collect a stable request trace (10k requests or 10 minutes).
2. Activate debug telemetry: set TELEMETRY_LEVEL=debug for the test pool.
3. Capture CPU and GPU counters: nsys (NVIDIA Nsight Systems) and ncu (Nsight Compute) profiles for representative iterations.
4. Capture in-process pprof and heap profiles (go/pytorch) and runtime logs with request-trace IDs.
5. Run microbenchmarks for kernels (see benchmarking suite below).

Commands and examples
- Collect live traces (staging):
  SSH to node: ssh -i ~/.ssh/runtime-staging deploy@staging-gpu-12
  Run nsys capture: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=trace.nsys ./bin/model-executor --config test-config.yaml --warmup 20 --iter 200
  Run ncu: ncu --target-processes all --set full --export sqlite --output ncu-report ./bin/model-executor --config test-config.yaml

- Extract pprof endpoint (Go exec): curl http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30 > cpu-profile.pb

What to look for
- Kernel launch latency: check average/95th kernel launch time in Nsight traces. Spiky launch times often indicate contention or small-batch fragmentation.
- CUDA memcpy hotspots: large host->device transfers indicate unbatched inputs or missing batching in the dispatcher.
- Warp efficiency and occupancy (ncu): low occupancy suggests kernel not using SMs effectively; consider different kernel variant or fusing ops.
- Garbage collection or CPU scheduling stalls: pprof aids identifying thread preemption or GC pauses.

Interpretation guide
- Small-batch fragmentation: signs are many small kernel launches with low utilization; fix by increasing batch_window_ms or tuning shard grouping.
- Memory contention: repeated OOMs or high memcpy; check max_batch_tokens, reduce per-request token cap, or enable model streaming.
- Tail latency spikes: correlate request traces to node-level CPU steal, noisy neighbors, or kernel fallback events.

4) Benchmarking suite (regression tests and capacity measurement)

Purpose
- Automated weekly regression tests for latency/throughput across critical models.
- On-demand capacity tests for sizing dedicated pools.

Key artifacts
- bench-runner: orchestrates microbenchmarks against a list of model images and kernel flags.
- bench-catalog: YAML of canonical test cases (model, seq_len, batch_sizes, token_lengths).
- results-store: time-series backend (Influx/Prometheus) and historical S3 bucket for raw JSON outputs.

Canonical bench cases (excerpt)
| id | model | seq_len | batch_sizes | metric |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| bench-1 | redwood/gpt-medium-fp16 | 128 | [1,4,8,16] | latency, throughput |
| bench-2 | redwood/gpt-large-4bit | 64 | [1,8,32] | latency, memory |
| bench-3 | redwood/seq2seq-encoder | 512 | [1,2,4] | latency, tail-latency |

How CI integrates
- Pull request gate: bench-runner unit tests + smoke microbench on small models.
- Nightly: full bench-catalog run against staging pool (resolves to known baseline).
- Weekly regression: run full catalog in a cut of production hardware; deviations >5% for latency or >10% throughput trigger a regression ticket.

Interpreting results and alerting
- CI compares median and p95 to baseline stored in results-store.
- Alerts: create incident if (median_latency_current / median_latency_baseline) >= 1.05 for >=3 contiguous runs or throughput <= 0.9 * baseline for >=2 runs.

Sample bench-runner command
- Run a single case locally: ./bin/bench-runner --case bench-1 --target staging --repeat 3 --output /tmp/bench-1.json

5) Release notes (runtime highlights, recent changes)

Recent notable releases (high-level)
- 2026-02-20: model-executor v2.3.0 — added fused-attention kernel for long context, improved warp utilization on sm90 GPUs, default quantized path for eligible models.
- 2026-01-10: runtime-dispatcher v1.9.1 — introduced preemption_threshold_ms and per-pool batch_window overrides.
- 2025-11-07: kv-cache v1.4 — added asynchronous Redis fallback to reduce cold-start misses.

Upgrade considerations
- Rolling upgrade strategy: drain node, update container image, run standard bench-catalog smoke, monitor metrics for 1 hour (latency, error-rate, GPU utl).
- Upgrade checklist (short):
  1) Notify oncall and affected customers.
  2) Drain target node: pause scheduling and wait for active shards to complete (max drain_timeout: 180s).
  3) Deploy image, kickoff bench-runner smoke.
  4) Gradual unpause and watch SLO dashboard for 30min.

6) Known issues (tracked and triaged)

Active items
- ISSUE-3214: sporadic 99p latency spikes for seq_len bucket 257-2048 on sm80 under mixed workloads. Root cause: kernel fusion fallback chosen incorrectly for some attention patterns. Mitigation: set allow_quantized=false on affected pool until patch (owner: eng-serving-runtime).
- ISSUE-2987: NVLink peer-to-peer errors observed on certain 8xA100 nodes after kernel upgrade. Workaround: reboot node and pin to previous kernel image; long-term: coordination with infra to replace faulty hardware (owner: eng-infra).

Backlog items
- Improve offline kernel selector to use cost-model based on observed occupancy.
- Add deterministic replay harness to reproduce tail-latency customer traces.

7) Runbooks (operational procedures)

Runbook: High tail latency (95p/99p spikes)
- Symptoms:
  - Console alerts: p95 or p99s exceed thresholds for 10+ mins
  - Traces show increased kernel launch times and many small batches
- Immediate actions:
  1) Verify alert: check SLO dashboard, confirm error-rate (prometheus query: rate(runtime_request_errors[5m]))
  2) Query affected pool and node list in console.
  3) If many small batches: increase batch_window_ms by 2x for the pool (set via admin API). Example API call:
     curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" -d '{"batch_window_ms":"16"}' https://console.internal/api/pools/example-pool/config
  4) If node-level noisy neighbor suspected: cordon and drain the node, fail-over shards.
  5) Collect Nsight and pprof profiles (see profiling playbook) and create an incident with traces attached.

Runbook: OOM or eviction on GPU node
- Symptoms:
  - Kubernetes OOMKilled events or CUDA out-of-memory logs
- Steps:
  1) Check pod logs and node dmesg.
  2) Reduce max_batch_tokens for the pool temporarily:
     curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" -d '{"max_batch_tokens":"2048"}' https://console.internal/api/pools/example-pool/config
  3) If OOM persists, cordon node and move shards to other nodes.
  4) Open a ticket to investigate model memory growth and recent kernel changes.

Runbook: Upgrade rollback
- When to use: production perf regression or functional break after upgrade.
- Steps:
  1) Stop new deployments and open incident.
  2) For each affected node: set desiredImage to previous-image:<tag> and drain to force redeploy.
  3) Run bench-runner smoke against redeployed nodes.
  4) Monitor SLOs for 2 hours before full resume.

8) Team wiki & knowledge links (how to contribute or find more)

How to propose a kernel change
1. Open an ADR in architecture-and-standards with a performance hypothesis and expected impact.
2. Create a feature branch and include microbenchmarks demonstrating benefit.
3. Submit PR with bench-runner results attached; request reviewers: @performance-team, @serving-runtime

Benchmark result interpretation guide
- Always compare to baseline run_id (available in results-store metadata). Attach raw JSON output to PR for auditability.

Templates and useful commands
- Create bench case template (bench-catalog entry):
  id: bench-x
  model: redwood/<model-name>
  seq_len: 128
  batch_sizes: [1,4,8]
  metrics: [latency,throughput,memory]

- Admin API examples:
  - Update pool config:
    curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" -d '{"batch_window_ms":"8","allow_quantized":"true"}' https://console.internal/api/pools/<pool>/config
  - Drain node:
    curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://console.internal/api/nodes/<node>/cordon

Appendix A: Useful Prometheus queries
- Current 95p latency for pool:
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket{pool="example-pool"}[5m])) by (le))
- Failed requests rate:
  sum(rate(runtime_request_errors_total[5m])) by (reason)

Appendix B: Benchmarks and sample output (abridged)
- bench-1 median latency: 48ms (baseline 45ms)
- bench-2 throughput: 9.3k tokens/sec (baseline 10.1k) -> regression alert created
- bench-3 99p latency: 210ms (within SLO)

Appendix C: Contacts and escalation
- Primary oncall: runtime-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Secondary: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Pager escalation: 15m -> 30m -> 60m to team leads
